name: Conciergerie
short_description: Medieval royal palace turned Revolutionary prison where Marie Antoinette and over 2,700 inmates were held during the Reign of Terror

beats.script_body: At no. 115 rue Saint-Honoré stood the pharmacy where the Swedish Marshal Fersen is believed to have obtained the invisible ink for his secret correspondence with Marie-Antoinette during her sequestration at the Conciergerie. A close friend of the royal family, Fersen had tried to help them escape from France. Evidence of the existence of the pharmacy goes back to 1715, making it one of the oldest in Paris.
beats.source_passage: the pharmacy where the Swedish Marshal Fersen is believed to have obtained the invisible ink for his correspondence with Marie-Antoinette during her sequestration at the Conciergerie

opening_hours_basis: Gated ticketed monument; transcribed from OSM tag 'Mo-Su 09:30-18:00'.
visit_basis: Medieval royal palace and Revolutionary prison; the vaulted Hall of the Men-at-Arms, the tribunal and Marie Antoinette's cell take around an hour plus a ticket queue.
judgement_basis: A medieval prison-monument requiring paid entry where quiet is expected indoors and there is no free seating, and the building locks at closing so no one can be left standing inside after dark.
queue_basis: Entry to the medieval prison passes through a security bag-check and a single ticket desk at one narrow entrance, so a substantial line forms midday and thins near opening and late afternoon.

name: Fontaine des Innocents
short_description: The only surviving Renaissance fountain in Paris, designed by Pierre Lescot and sculpted by Jean Goujon in 1549 for Henri II's entry into the city

beats.script_body: The Fontaine des Innocents at Place Joachim du Bellay is the only Renaissance fountain surviving in Paris. Designed by architect Pierre Lescot and sculpted by Jean Goujon — the greatest sculptor of his time — it was inaugurated on 16 June 1549 for Henri II's solemn entry into the city. Originally the fountain stood at the corner of rue Saint-Denis and the present rue Berger, against the church of Saints-Innocents, and had three arcades with a balcony where prominent figures took shelter during royal processions. The fountain commemorates the old Cimetière des Innocents that occupied this site until 1787, when the cemetery was replaced by a colourful fruit, vegetable and herb market. The church of Saints-Innocents was demolished when the cemetery closed. The market itself was demolished in 1855, and the fountain was shifted, altered and restored to its present location.
beats.source_passage: the only Renaissance fountain in Paris, was designed by Pierre Lescot and sculpted by Jean Goujon in 1549, the greatest sculptor of his time

opening_hours_basis: A Renaissance fountain standing in an open public square, viewed from the pavement, so not gated.
visit_basis: Single Renaissance fountain in a pedestrian square, sculpted reliefs to walk round; a monument with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A pedestrian square around a fountain with hard paving and steps but no enclosure or barrier from surrounding streets so running is unsafe, though the steps offer free seating and the busy Les Halles area is lit and peopled after dark.
queue_basis: A Renaissance fountain standing in an open square with no interior or gate, so there is nothing to queue for.

name: Les Halles
short_description: Site of Paris's central food market for 800 years from 1135 until its controversial demolition in 1969, now the Forum des Halles shopping centre

beats.script_body: In the 13th century, rue de la Ferronnerie — just steps from Les Halles — was the stronghold of the iron trade after which it was named: a narrow, congested street cluttered with blacksmiths' and ironmongers' stalls. It was still much the same on 14 May 1610 when the royal coach carrying Henri IV was held up in traffic on his way from the Louvre to the Arsenal near the Bastille, where his minister Sully was residing. The King was absorbed in a letter when a man named Ravaillac jumped onto the coach and stabbed him to death. Ravaillac was declared mentally deranged but was nevertheless sentenced to be drawn and quartered on Place de Grève — today's Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville — a sentence speedily carried out just thirteen days after the crime.
beats.source_passage: a man named Ravaillac jumped on to the coach and stabbed him. The assassin was declared mentally deranged but was nevertheless sentenced to be quartered

beats.script_body: At no. 93 rue Saint-Honoré, an apothecary bore witness to two of France's most traumatic royal events across nearly two centuries. An apothecary was already trading here on 14 May 1610, when Henri IV was stabbed by Ravaillac on the neighbouring rue de la Ferronnerie. One hundred and eighty-three years later, on the day of Marie-Antoinette's execution on 16 October 1793, the successor apothecary at the same address closed his shop 'Au Bourdon d'Or' as a sign of mourning.
beats.source_passage: An earlier apothecary was trading here on 14 May 1610, when Henri IV was stabbed on the neighbouring rue de la Ferronnerie

beats.script_body: The corner house at 2 rue Sauval, in the heart of Les Halles, was the birthplace of Molière in 1622 — the playwright whose stormy funeral at Saint-Eustache nearby would one day require the King's personal intervention. The original house was later demolished and replaced by the one still standing today, where the composer Richard Wagner reportedly stayed in 1839.
beats.source_passage: The corner house at 2 rue Sauval... was the birthplace of Moliére in 1622. The house was later demolished and replaced by the one still standing today, where Wagner stayed in 1839

beats.script_body: At the corner of rue Vauvilliers, near Les Halles, the first episode of the Fronde — the revolt against Louis XIV's mentor and Minister, Cardinal Mazarin — began in August 1648.
beats.source_passage: the corner of rue Vauvilliers where the first episode of the Fronde, the revolt against Louis XIV's mentor and Minister, Mazarin, began in August 1648

beats.script_body: Outside Saint-Eustache, the streets of rue du Jour, rue Montmartre and rue Montorgueil have retained the atmosphere of the old Les Halles market. Although trendy boutiques are gradually taking over, they have not yet ousted the colourful displays of food that spill into the streets — mainly on rue Montorgueil — ravishing the eye and delighting the palate. Nearby, at no. 6 rue Coquillère, Le Pied de Cochon has preserved its Belle Époque setting and still serves its famous onion soup.
beats.source_passage: trendy boutiques are gradually taking over, they have not as yet ousted the colourful displays of food that spill into the streets

opening_hours_basis: Named as a historic market site and present-day district setting rather than an entered venue, so treated as an open urban setting and not gated.
visit_basis: Site of the former market, now the Forum des Halles with its Canopy roof and surrounding gardens; the mall interior and levels absorb around 40 min if entered.
judgement_basis: A large shopping-centre-and-garden complex where children cannot run free among crowds and roads, but the surrounding Nelson Mandela garden has free benches and lawns quiet enough to talk, and the area is lit and busy well into the night.
queue_basis: The Forum des Halles is an open shopping centre with multiple free entrances and no admission control, so nobody waits to enter.

name: Place de la Concorde
short_description: Largest square in Paris where over 1,300 people were guillotined in a single month during the 1794 Reign of Terror

beats.script_body: For a brief period, rue Saint-Honoré became the sinister route of the tumbrils on their way from the Conciergerie prison to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution — today's Place de la Concorde. On 16 October 1793, the painter Jacques-Louis David positioned himself on a corner house balcony at rue des Prouvaires and 54 rue Saint-Honoré, from where he had a clear view of Marie-Antoinette carried to her doom, her hands tied behind her back — a tragic sight he captured in his shattering portrait of the Queen. On the same day, the apothecary at no. 93 rue Saint-Honoré closed his shop 'Au Bourdon d'Or' as a sign of mourning — a quiet gesture in a city gripped by revolutionary justice.
beats.source_passage: the painter David was posted on the corner house balcony of rue des Prouvaires... from where he had a good view of Marie-Antoinette carried to her doom, her hands tied behind her back

opening_hours_basis: Open public square viewed and crossed freely from the pavement; not gated.
visit_basis: The largest square in Paris with the Luxor obelisk, two fountains and views toward the Tuileries and the Champs-Elysees; walking between its positions absorbs 35 minutes, with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A huge open square ringed and crossed by heavy fast traffic with no barrier and no quiet free seating, so a child cannot safely run and conversation is drowned; it is brightly lit and busy at all hours, so a person left standing is fine.
queue_basis: An open public square with no interior, door, or ticket, so there is no line to stand in.

anchors.label: The obelisk
anchors.basis: The Luxor obelisk is the centre of the square and the corpus speaks of the very spot where Louis XVI was beheaded; a person stands on the traffic island around its pedestal to look up at the hieroglyphs and the gold pictures. Sixty metres covers the island and the crossings onto it and keeps the claim off the square's outer footways half a footprint away.

name: Pont Neuf
short_description: Oldest surviving bridge in Paris built in 1578, the first stone bridge without houses on it, with 381 carved grotesque faces

beats.script_body: Henri IV's early amorous adventures had gained him the affectionate nickname 'le Vert Galant' — the amorous youth. But the charm faded as he grew older. The population resented the fact that he had at least eleven illegitimate children scattered throughout the kingdom, which all but plunged France into civil strife yet again. Furthermore, he had expressed his intention to marry his favourite mistress, Gabrielle d'Estrées — an outrage to the raison d'état. Only her premature death prevented this infamy. As Femme Ladoucette, a Dame des Halles, had expressed it in her letter to the Queen: in the kingdom of France, one separated the sheep from the goats. The assassination on rue de la Ferronnerie in 1610 was not the first attempt on the King's life — his scandalous personal conduct had made him many enemies.
beats.source_passage: his early amorous adventures had gained him the affectionate nickname of le Vert Galant (the amorous youth), the charm faded as he grew older

opening_hours_basis: Open street bridge crossable at any hour, not gated.
visit_basis: Oldest bridge in Paris with 381 carved grotesque faces and river views from its bays; a destination to walk across and pause on but nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A stone road bridge with traffic down the middle and parapets straight onto the river where a running child is in danger, and its half-moon stone bays sit metres from moving cars making conversation an effort, but it is lit, open and centrally crossed at all hours.
queue_basis: A public bridge with no door and no ticket; the whole value stands in the open and there is no line.

anchors.label: Place Dauphine
anchors.basis: The triangular square opens off the bridge's mid-river terrace behind the Henri IV statue; a person steps off the bridge and stands inside the triangle to look at the brick-and-stone houses the corpus tells. Half the footprint reaches from the statue's steps into the square.

anchors.label: The Henri IV statue
anchors.basis: The bronze horseman stands on the terre-plein at the bridge's middle, directly above the steps down to the square du Vert-Galant — one standing position for both named spots, and a person looks at the statue from the platform around it.
